title: Failover economics & contract readiness - Argent Holdings
summary: Initial reliability and contracting intake to surface Argent's failover requirements, SLA expectations, and hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs. Focus on multi-region routing, failover economics, and legal contract readiness.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-19 15:00 UTC | Duration 52m | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Marta Cheng (CTO, Argent), Devon Park (Head of Platform), Liam O'Connor (SRE Lead), Sana Qureshi (Legal Ops)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Priya, our site reliability engineer. How are we doing?
[00:12] Marta Cheng: Good, hi. Thanks for squeezing us in. We have a tight procurement window so want to be fairly concrete today.
[00:18] Devon Park: Yep, timeline's important. We've got budget committee meeting in two weeks.
[00:23] Jordan Lee: Understood. High level today we'll walk through reliability/failover patterns, how Redwood handles region and model fallbacks, and then align on SLA needs and any contract asks. Priya will tackle the technical bits.
[00:32] Priya Raman: Hi all. Quick note — I'll speak to routing, KV cache and what we call prefix caching, and typical latency profiles across hosted/dedicated/private.
[00:40] Liam O'Connor: Good. We want to understand failure modes — region outage, partial degradation, and also the economics. If you force region failover, what's unit cost impact and how does billing work?
[00:51] Jordan Lee: Great question. We'll cover pricing delta for cross-region egress, reserved dedicated pools, and fallbacks to cheaper model variants.
[00:58] Sana Qureshi: From legal, we'll need to know SLA credits and audit evidence — SOC2 reports, KMS/HSM integration details, and whether you can commit to data residency in EU for certain workloads.
[01:10] Priya Raman: On the technical side, typical pattern: requests route to nearest region by latency. When capacity or a region fails, Redwood can do automated fallback to a secondary region, or to a lower-cost model variant with identical API surface. There are tradeoffs: cross-region adds network latency, and model variant fallbacks can change output quality.
[01:34] Devon Park: When you say lower-cost model variants, are those quantized variants, or smaller architectures?
[01:38] Priya Raman: Both. We have quantized builds (8-bit/4-bit) and alternate architectures we verify. We surface estimated quality delta in the catalog, but you can pin critical routes to avoid fallback.
[01:48] Marta Cheng: Pinning looks appealing but we need predictable throughput for peak loads. How do dedicated pools behave under full rack failure?
[01:55] Priya Raman: Dedicated runs on reserved GPU pools. If a rack fails, autoscaling can spill to a separate pool or region if configured. We recommend multi-AZ within a region — but for true region failure you need multi-region pools or the hosted fallback.
[02:10] Liam O'Connor: So multi-region is an explicit configuration. If we enable it, does Redwood replicate KV caches across regions? How quickly is warmup?
[02:18] Priya Raman: We have a couple strategies: active-active with synchronous KV replication (higher cost), active-passive with async warming, and prefix/KV cache seeding for common prompts. Warmup depends on your prompt set size; with seeding you can hit good hit rates in a few minutes for known prefixes.
[02:35] Devon Park: A few minutes is ok for many flows. For auth flows we need near-zero failover time.
[02:40] Jordan Lee: For those high-sensitivity paths we usually recommend dedicated capacity with a hot standby in a second region and can set higher replication. That comes with a committed capacity delta.
[02:50] Martha (mislabelled)? [Speaker tag glitch] Marta Cheng: Sorry, Jordan, quick clarifying — what's the expected RTO/RPO you guarantee in the SLA for hosted customers?
[02:58] Jordan Lee: Our SLA we typically discuss: 99.95% monthly uptime for hosted API for production-tier customers; dedicated can be bumped to 99.99% depending on contract. RTO for region failover is contextual — automatic routing failover is under 60s for routing-level, but warmed caches and model loading can add variable time.
[03:18] Liam O'Connor: That 60s number—what does it include? Is that DNS-level steering or routing at the load balancer?
[03:24] Priya Raman: It's internal routing detection plus steering between regions. DNS propagation is not in the critical path — we use our edge routers and health checks to route. Still, model cold-start may add seconds to tens of seconds depending on model size.
[03:38] Devon Park: Can you do pre-warmed standby for large models?
[03:41] Priya Raman: Yes, in dedicated we can keep warm instances and even reserve GPU memory for KV caches. This affects pricing — it's reserved capacity.
[03:49] Marta Cheng: On the economics — can you show a delta in cost for: hosted single-region, hosted multi-region with async caching, dedicated single-region, and dedicated multi-region hot standby?
[03:59] Jordan Lee: We'll follow up with a small spreadsheet. Off the cuff: multi-region hot standby can multiply committed cost by ~1.6-2x depending on model footprint, while async multi-region is more like +20–40% on per-token cost due to cross-region egress and lower cache hits.
[04:17] Devon Park: That's a big swing. How do we model that for 99.99% SLA with 500 qps?
[04:22] Priya Raman: We can run a quick capacity calc post-call — need your average tokens per request, percent of hot traffic, and model choice.
[04:29] Liam O'Connor: Tokens per request varies—auth flows ~30 tokens, docs summarization ~800 tokens. We'll share a breakdown.
[04:36] Jordan Lee: That helps.
[04:38] Sana Qureshi: Legal — on penalties. Do you include financial credits or termination rights for repeated SLA misses? We have a procurement playbook that requires credits for sustained outages.
[04:48] Jordan Lee: Standard is service credits ladder tied to monthly uptime. For enterprise we can discuss customized remedies; termination for repeated breaches tends to be negotiated for enterprise deals. We'll flag this with our contracts team.
[04:59] Marta Cheng: Also need to confirm encryption at rest and KMS — can we bring our own KMS?
[05:05] Priya Raman: Yes, Redwood Private and Dedicated support customer-managed keys (BYOK) via KMS/HSM integrations. Hosted can integrate with customer KMS in many cases; we'll pull the security note for specifics.
[05:16] Devon Park: Regarding private deployments: we operate in a restrictive environment — air-gapped staging, SOC2 plus additional attestation. Do you support on-prem package?
[05:25] Jordan Lee: Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages. On-prem installs require coordination, licensing, and a security questionnaire. For regulated workloads, that's our recommendation.
[05:34] Liam O'Connor: If we go Private, does Redwood still provide the control plane or is that a customer-managed control plane?
[05:40] Priya Raman: We offer both: customer-managed control plane for full isolation, or a hybrid where telemetry is forwarded to Redwood but data stores remain in your VPC. That choice affects observability and support paths.
[05:51] Devon Park: In hybrid, how do you handle tracing and cost telemetry without sending PII?
[05:57] Priya Raman: We redact payloads and provide token-level cost breakdowns while preserving privacy. We can also provide aggregated traces only.
[06:06] Marta Cheng: Ok, let's walk through some failure scenarios — 1) full region outage 2) model deployment bug causing 50% latency increase 3) degraded KV cache causing 2x token cost. What's your recommended default behavior for each?
[06:18] Priya Raman: 1) Full region outage: route to secondary region (if enabled) and optionally fallback to a compatible model variant if capacity constrained. 2) Model bug: automatic circuit breaker and fallback to previous stable model version, alerting and canary rollback. 3) KV cache degradation: we throttle batching and can enable cost-protect mode that reduces concurrency and increases batching to reduce per-token unit cost — that saves dollars but increases latency.
[06:46] Liam O'Connor: That cost-protect mode sounds useful — but who triggers it? Is it automatic or manual?
[06:50] Priya Raman: It can be automatic via policies you configure (degradation thresholds) or manual via the console / API.
[06:58] Devon Park: For canary rollouts, can Redwood do traffic splits by header or customer ID? We have tenant-specific constraints.
[07:04] Priya Raman: Yes — we support route-based splitting (by header, path, or customer ID). Canary policies can do gradual ramp and automatic rollback on error budget breach.
[07:12] Jordan Lee: Quick note — we often recommend dev/prod separation with different fallback policies.
[07:17] Marta Cheng: On observability, we need per-request latency histograms and token-level cost in our own dashboard. Can we pull raw telemetry to Splunk/Datadog?
[07:25] Priya Raman: We have integrations for Datadog, Prometheus, and can export logs to S3 for Splunk ingestion. For token-level billing, we provide detailed CSVs or API endpoints.
[07:36] Sana Qureshi: Another legal question — audit logs. We need user-level access logs for compliance. Retention must be 7 years in our jurisdiction. Can Redwood retain logs that long?
[07:46] Jordan Lee: Our standard retention is 90 days for hosted, but we offer extended retention add-ons for enterprise, and Private can be configured for your retention policy. We'll include retention options in follow-up.
[07:57] Liam O'Connor: Is there an offline mode? Like if connectivity to Redwood control plane fails, can our local inference continue?
[08:03] Priya Raman: In Private we can run fully offline inference with customer control plane. Hosted and dedicated depend on control plane connectivity; some local caching helps but not full operation.
[08:13] Devon Park: Let's talk about contractual SLAs again — for 99.99% can you commit to performance SLAs (p95 latency < 150ms for auth flows) or is that a best-effort?
[08:24] Jordan Lee: We can commit to latency SLOs in dedicated contracts with specific hardware guarantees and benchmarked profiles. Hosted is more variable; we publish performance profiles per model but strict latency SLAs are usually part of Dedicated/enterprise terms.
[08:39] Marta Cheng: How do you measure p95? Is that across all tenants or per-customer? Per-customer is what procurement wants.
[08:46] Priya Raman: We can provide per-customer p95 metrics with token and route breakdown in Dedicated and Private. For hosted, we provide aggregated metrics but can export per-token traces on request.
[08:58] Jordan Lee: Quick interjection — competitors. Do you evaluate any other vendors right now?
[09:02] Marta Cheng: We have a short list: OpenAI for hosted, Anthropic for safety features, and our internal self-hosted Triton pipeline for sensitive data.
[09:10] Jordan Lee: Good to know.
[09:12] Devon Park: Back to cost modeling — if a multi-region failover occurs and we fall back to a cheaper model variant, do you annotate responses as downgraded so downstream can treat them differently?
[09:22] Priya Raman: Yes — Redwood can include metadata in the response headers/body indicating model variant used and fallback reason. That helps downstream feature flags.
[09:31] Liam O'Connor: We need that for auditability.
[09:33] Priya Raman: Also you can route only specific routes to fallbacks and keep others pinned.
[09:39] Marta Cheng: For the pilot we want to simulate regional outage. Can Redwood help with chaos testing or a runbook?
[09:46] Jordan Lee: Yes, we have a runbook and can run joint chaos drills. We can simulate region failover, cache degradation, and model rollout failures. We'll propose dates for a pilot stress window.
[09:56] Devon Park: Great. Who needs to be involved from Redwood for that pilot?
[10:00] Jordan Lee: SE + SRE + Solutions Architect typically. Priya will be the SE lead.
[10:06] Priya Raman: I'll coordinate the technical plan.
[10:09] Marta Cheng: Ok, timeline constraints — procurement meeting in two weeks. We need: 1) a pricing delta sheet 2) proposed SLA language 3) security pack (SOC2, KMS matrix, network diagrams) 4) a pilot runbook. Can you deliver those in 5 business days?
[10:23] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll aim for 3–5 business days. We'll prioritize pricing spreadsheet and SLA draft.
[10:29] Sana Qureshi: Also want a sample contract clause for credits and termination for SLA non-performance.
[10:33] Jordan Lee: Noted. We'll include suggested contract language.
[10:36] Devon Park: On the pilot — can we do a week-long ramp with traffic mirroring and a single failover drill?
[10:42] Priya Raman: Absolutely. Mirror traffic is standard; we can do a controlled failover test mid-week.
[10:47] Marta Cheng: Onboarding questions — how long to onboard a dedicated pool?
[10:50] Jordan Lee: Dedicated pools typically provision in 2–4 weeks depending on commit and region availability. Private/on-prem take longer — that's usually 6–12 weeks.
[10:59] Liam O'Connor: Can you provide an SSO/SAML integration guide? Our identity team needs that.
[11:03] Priya Raman: We'll attach SSO docs.
[11:05] Jordan Lee: Quick note on billing — multi-region egress and reserved standby are line-items. We'll make the cost sheet explicit.
[11:11] Devon Park: For the pilot, we'd prefer hosted with dedicated burst capacity. Is burst possible without long-term commit?
[11:17] Priya Raman: Yes we have burst options for hosted, but guaranteed throughput for peak needs Dedicated. Burst is subject to availability.
[11:23] Marta Cheng: Any concerns about data residency? Our EU customers' data must remain in EU. Can hosted enforce per-tenant region residency?
[11:31] Jordan Lee: We support per-tenant region pinning for hosted and Dedicated. Private gives you full residency control.
[11:37] Sana Qureshi: On audit logs retention — can you give an estimated cost for 7-year retention?
[11:42] Jordan Lee: We'll include retention pricing in the follow-up.
[11:46] Liam O'Connor: One more technical nuance — when fallback occurs, do you preserve session context and KV cache consistency?
[11:53] Priya Raman: Session context is preserved at the request level, but deep KV cache consistency across regions is eventual; we avoid silent divergence by tagging responses with cache-hit metadata. For strict consistency, synchronous replication is needed.
[12:05] Devon Park: Anything else on tooling for rollback?
[12:08] Priya Raman: Rollbacks are versioned and can be automated with canary policies. We also support manual aborts.
[12:14] Jordan Lee: Let's move to a quick recap and next steps.
[12:17] Jordan Lee: Recap: we aligned on pilot, onboarding timeline, deliverables (pricing sheet, SLA draft, security pack, runbook). Pilot scope: hosted with burst or dedicated reserved standby depending on cost. We will surface modeled delta for 500 qps and token profiles you send.
[12:34] Marta Cheng: That sounds right. We will send token profile and traffic splits by EOD tomorrow.
[12:40] Devon Park: We'll also include a list of routes with strict pinning requirements.
[12:44] Sana Qureshi: Legal will review SLA clauses — expect comments.
[12:48] Jordan Lee: Action owners — Jordan to send pricing and SLA draft; Priya to produce pilot runbook and technical checklist; Contracts to follow up on credits language.
[12:57] Jordan Lee: Any other questions?
[12:59] Liam O'Connor: One small ask — can you add an annotation flag in responses for fallback reason in our pilot?
[13:04] Priya Raman: Yes — we'll include a header and optional body field for fallback annotation.
[13:09] Marta Cheng: Thank you. We'll look for materials.
[13:12] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deliverables and schedule the pilot kickoff.
[13:17] End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: There are occasional speaker label mismatches; some technical terms transcribed as "K V cash" or "quantize eight bit". Natural speech artifacts retained.
